mcqs.question: Your team wants a defensible pass/fail answer for Core Web Vitals. What is the correct basis for that decision?
options: A single Lighthouse run against the production URL on the desktop preset
The 75th percentile of field data for each metric, assessed per metric and segmented by mobile and desktop
The average of LCP, INP, and CLS values collected in RUM, reported as one score
The median FID from the most recent CrUX period
mcqs.explanation: Core Web Vitals pass/fail is a field-data question: each metric is assessed on its distribution at the 75th percentile, and mobile and desktop are segmented rather than blended (https://web.dev/articles/vitals). The single Lighthouse run is the strongest distractor because Lighthouse is genuinely useful, but it is one controlled lab run, not a substitute for what real users experienced. Averaging hides the tail that the p75 exists to expose, and blending three metrics into one score has no meaning in the assessment. The FID option reaches for a metric that was replaced by INP as the responsiveness vital (https://web.dev/articles/inp), and a median is the wrong statistic anyway.

mcqs.question: Field data shows poor LCP on a product page. The LCP element is a text block rendered on the client after hydration. Which fix most directly targets the dominant phase?
options: Convert the hero image to AVIF and cut its bytes by 70%
Preload the hero image so it arrives earlier
Reduce render delay: serve the content server-rendered and remove render-blocking work so the text paints earlier
Add loading="lazy" to below-the-fold images
mcqs.explanation: LCP time is the sum of TTFB, resource-load delay, resource-load duration, and render delay (https://web.dev/articles/lcp). When the LCP element is text that only appears after client-side rendering or hydration, the dominant phase is render delay, so server-rendering the content and reducing render-blocking work attacks the measured problem. Image compression is the strongest distractor because it is the reflex LCP fix, but the LCP element is not an image, so its bytes are irrelevant here. Preloading the hero image optimizes a resource that is not the LCP element, and lazy-loading below-the-fold images helps offscreen network work but does nothing for when the largest text block first renders.

mcqs.question: A page loads two classic scripts in the head: vendor.js (large, no dependencies) and app.js (depends on vendor.js). Order matters and both are needed to initialize the UI. What is the correct loading setup?
options: Both async: downloads run in parallel and execution order does not matter
app.js defer, vendor.js async: the small one waits, the big one does not
Both defer: downloads run in parallel, document order is preserved, and both run after parsing
Leave both without attributes: parser-blocking guarantees correctness, so it is the safest choice
mcqs.explanation: defer downloads both scripts in parallel, preserves document order, and executes after HTML parsing, which satisfies both the dependency and the ordering requirement while removing parser blocking. The both-async option is the strongest distractor because async also parallelizes downloads, but async executes each script as soon as it is ready with no order guarantee, so app.js can run before vendor.js and throw. The mixed defer/async setup still allows app.js to execute before vendor.js has run. Leaving both parser-blocking is correct but slow: classic scripts without attributes serialize fetch and execution and stall DOM construction. Module scripts are an alternative since they are deferred by default and can encode the dependency with an import.

mcqs.question: Which loading setup best serves a product page with a large hero image (the likely LCP element) and a grid of below-the-fold related-product images?
options: loading="lazy" on every image including the hero, to minimize initial network work
Hero as a CSS background-image so it does not block parsing; grid images eager
Every image eager but heavily compressed, so nothing is ever deferred
Hero eager with intrinsic dimensions and responsive sources; grid images loading="lazy" with dimensions
mcqs.explanation: The likely LCP image must be eager, discoverable in the HTML, sized with responsive sources, and carry intrinsic dimensions, while below-the-fold images are the correct target for loading="lazy" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Performance/Guides/Lazy_loading). The lazy-everything option is the strongest distractor because it looks like a clean audit win, but deferring the LCP image delays the very metric it feeds. The CSS background-image option trades a real problem for a worse one: a background image is discovered only after the stylesheet is fetched and parsed, adding resource-load delay to the likely LCP (https://web.dev/learn/performance/resource-hints). The all-eager option wastes mobile bandwidth by sending desktop-sized bytes and forgoes deferral where it is free.

mcqs.question: A team preloads their self-hosted critical font with `<link rel="preload" href="/app-sans.woff2" as="font">`. The waterfall shows the font downloading twice. Why?
options: Preload does not work for font files; only scripts and stylesheets can be preloaded
The preload is missing crossorigin: fonts are fetched in CORS mode even when self-hosted, so the hinted request does not match the CSS's request and the browser downloads the font again
woff2 cannot be preloaded; the team should switch to woff
The font file must be base64-inlined into the CSS to avoid a second download
mcqs.explanation: Fonts are CORS resources, so a font preload must include crossorigin and match the URL the stylesheet requests; otherwise the preload is not reused and the font is fetched twice (https://web.dev/learn/performance/optimize-web-fonts). The 'preload does not work for fonts' option is the strongest distractor because it sounds like a plausible hint limitation, but fonts are one of the most common and recommended preload use cases. The woff2 option invents a format restriction that does not exist; woff2 is the recommended web font format. Base64-inlining the font would avoid the second request by making the CSS enormous, which delays other critical work.

mcqs.question: After aggressive per-route splitting, initial JavaScript dropped to 60KB, but opening the settings route now feels slower than before the split. What is the most likely cause?
options: The settings UI waits on a chain of small chunks fetched sequentially, and shared dependencies may be duplicated across them
Modern browsers cannot cache small chunks efficiently, so every navigation re-downloads them
Dynamic import() is inherently slower than a static import at runtime
The entry bundle is still too large for the route to initialize
mcqs.explanation: Splitting is harmful when critical UI waits on a chain of tiny chunks or when shared dependencies are duplicated: a smaller entry bundle is not automatically a faster task if it adds late blocking requests (https://webpack.js.org/guides/code-splitting/). The 'entry bundle is still too large' option is the strongest distractor because entry size is the number everyone watches, but the premise says it dropped to 60KB; the cost moved to the route's load path. The browser-caching option misattributes the problem to caching, which handles small chunks fine when cache headers are correct. The import() option blames the import mechanism, which is cheap; the cost is the extra round trips and duplicated code the boundaries created.

mcqs.question: Analytics shows users of the dashboard route almost always visit the settings route next. The team wants the settings chunk available for that next navigation without competing with the current route's critical resources. Which approach fits?
options: Preload the settings chunk: it starts in parallel with the current chunk at higher urgency
Inline the settings chunk into the entry bundle so it is always present
Prefetch the settings chunk: it is fetched after the parent chunk finishes, during idle time
Do nothing and fetch the chunk on click: the network is fast enough
mcqs.explanation: A prefetch targets a credible future navigation: in webpack's model the prefetched chunk waits until the parent finishes and is fetched during idle time, so it does not compete with the current navigation's critical work (https://webpack.js.org/guides/code-splitting/). The preload option is the strongest distractor because preload also fetches early, but preload is for resources needed during the current navigation and runs at higher urgency in parallel with the parent, which is exactly the bandwidth competition the team wants to avoid. Inlining into the entry bloats every dashboard visit with code that other routes never need. Fetching on click forfeits the observed user path and pays the chunk latency on every transition.

mcqs.question: A team virtualizes a 200-item list to improve INP on row clicks, but field INP is unchanged. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The list needs more overscan to cover the interaction window
Virtualization limits DOM size but does not make each row's handler or render work cheaper; the bottleneck was likely elsewhere
The virtualization library itself is the bottleneck; switching libraries will fix it
INP only measures the first interaction on the page, and that one was already fast
mcqs.explanation: Virtualization reduces rendering, style, and interaction work that scales with DOM size, but it does not make each row cheaper; if the demonstrated bottleneck is the row's own handler or something else entirely, windowing moves nothing (https://web.dev/articles/dom-size-and-interactivity). Profile before virtualizing and use it when list size is the demonstrated bottleneck. The 'INP only measures the first interaction' option is the strongest distractor because it reaches for a real-sounding metric fact, but it describes FID, which only measured the first interaction's input delay; INP observes interactions across the page lifetime (https://web.dev/articles/inp). The overscan option tunes a scroll-smoothing parameter that has nothing to do with click latency. The library option blames the tool before establishing that DOM size was ever the problem.

mcqs.question: Lighthouse in CI reports 95+ for a route, but CrUX shows the mobile segment failing LCP. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Use the field data to confirm the affected segment, then reproduce with a throttled, mobile-like lab trace to isolate the cause
Trust Lighthouse: CrUX is noisy field data and the lab run is controlled
Trust CrUX alone and roll back the last release that touched the route
Run Lighthouse five more times and report the best score
mcqs.explanation: Lab and field answer different questions: field data identifies the affected population and prioritizes user impact, and lab traces reproduce and isolate the cause under controlled conditions (https://web.dev/articles/lab-and-field-data-differences). The 'trust Lighthouse' option is the strongest distractor because 'controlled' sounds like 'more trustworthy', but the lab's device, network, and cache choices may simply not match the failing mobile population. Rolling back on CrUX alone acts on field data without a diagnosis and reverts code that may not be the cause. Repeated Lighthouse runs are cherry-picking: they still measure the same unrepresentative scenario.

mcqs.question: A loop updates 500 rows by reading row.getBoundingClientRect().height and then writing row.style.top and row.style.left, one row at a time. The interaction is janky. Which fix addresses the root cause?
options: Wrap each iteration in requestAnimationFrame so the browser batches it
Hoist all geometry reads before all writes: collect the measurements first, then apply the position changes in a second pass
Replace the transform-based approach with top and left so the browser avoids transform math
Move the loop into a web worker so it runs off the main thread
mcqs.explanation: The loop interleaves layout reads with style writes: after each write the layout is dirty, so the next read forces a Recalculate Style and Layout pass, 500 times per interaction. Batching all reads before all writes collapses that to one layout (https://web.dev/articles/avoid-large-complex-layouts-and-layout-thrashing). The requestAnimationFrame option is the strongest distractor because rAF sounds like a batching primitive, but it only schedules when the callback runs; the read-write interleaving inside the callback thrashes exactly the same. The top/left option makes things worse: writing top and left triggers layout on every write, while transforms avoid it. The worker option is impossible: DOM APIs do not exist in workers.

mcqs.question: Which performance-budget design is most likely to actually change what teams build?
options: A single global JavaScript byte cap for the whole site, reviewed in a monthly report
A Lighthouse performance-score floor of 90 enforced in CI
Budgets owned and applied identically by the platform team across every route

Route- and device-class-specific budgets combining quantity caps (JS and image bytes, request count, third-party cost) with user-centric metrics (LCP, INP, CLS), enforced in CI and monitored in field, where every exception carries an owner, expiry, and reason
mcqs.explanation: Budgets that change behavior are tied to a route, device class, and user task; they combine quantity budgets with user-centric metrics, are set from a measured baseline, are enforced in CI for repeatable lab signals, and are monitored in field distributions after release, because a passing synthetic budget can still hide a real-user regression (https://web.dev/articles/performance-budgets-101). The global byte cap is the strongest distractor because it is easy to communicate, but it is not tied to any user task, so it either blocks necessary routes or excuses wasteful ones. The score floor proxies everything through one lab number. Identical platform-owned budgets ignore route context, the same failure mode as centralizing resource hints without it.

scenarios.prompt: This reorder animation runs at roughly 12fps on mid-range phones, and a Performance trace shows one long task with repeated Recalculate Style and Layout entries. Diagnose the root cause and rewrite the function so the interaction stays smooth. Explain what the trace should look like after the fix.
rubric: Identifies forced layout: the read-after-write interleaving forces Recalculate Style and Layout per row, not once per frame
Batches all geometry reads before all writes instead of reaching for rAF or debounce wrappers
Replaces top/left with transform so movement no longer triggers layout
Mentions caching measurements or reducing the affected DOM for repeated interactions
Verifies the fix by re-recording the same trace scenario and comparing the user-facing metric

scenarios.prompt: Predict what happens at runtime with this document, explain the failure mode and when it occurs, then rewrite the script loading so the page initializes reliably without blocking parsing more than necessary.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Prediction: analytics.js is a classic script with no attribute, so it blocks HTML parsing while it is fetched and executed, delaying DOM construction for a script that has no dependency on the document. vendor.js and app.js are async: they download in parallel, but each executes as soon as it has downloaded, with no order guarantee. app.js is smaller than vendor.js, so on a cold cache it frequently finishes first, executes, and calls window.Vendor.render before vendor.js has run, throwing a ReferenceError and leaving the page blank. The failure is intermittent by construction: with a warm cache, or when vendor.js happens to win the race, the page works, which is why it survives testing. Fix: analytics.js is independent, so it should be async. vendor.js and app.js have a dependency and an ordering requirement, so both should be defer: parallel download, document order preserved, execution after parsing. An even better shape is modules, which are deferred by default and encode the dependency explicitly:

```html
<script async src="/analytics.js"></script>
<script type="module" src="/app.js"></script>
```

with app.js importing vendor. Then confirm the actual request and execution order in the Network and Performance panels rather than trusting the attributes.
rubric: Predicts the ReferenceError: async does not preserve execution order, so app.js can execute before vendor.js
Explains why the bug is intermittent (cache and network races), which is why it survives testing
Identifies analytics.js as parser-blocking and makes it async since it is independent
Uses defer, or modules with an explicit import, for the dependent pair so order is preserved without blocking parsing
Verifies the final request and execution order in the Network and Performance panels

scenarios.prompt: This field-vitals instrumentation shipped to production. The team's dashboard disagrees with CrUX, and a large share of pageviews never reports anything. Identify at least three distinct problems with the measurement design and rewrite the snippet.
rubric: Recognizes CLS is not a raw sum and replaces the hand-rolled math with onCLS and its defined aggregation rules
Moves reporting to visibilitychange (page hidden) in addition to unload, explaining why unload loses samples
Adds route, release, and device context so regressions can be segmented and acted on
Spots the missing buffered observation for entries recorded before the observer existed
Keeps the reference implementation as the source of metric semantics instead of reimplementing them

scenarios.prompt: After a redesign, this product page regressed LCP and CLS in field data, worst on mobile. Audit the loading strategy in the component, explain each problem and which metric it hurts, and refactor it.
rubric: Moves the hero out of a CSS background-image into an HTML img/picture so it is discoverable during the initial parse
Serves responsive sources instead of one desktop-sized asset to every device
Adds intrinsic dimensions (or an aspect ratio) to every image to reserve layout space and prevent CLS
Defers below-the-fold images with loading="lazy" so they stop competing with the hero's bandwidth
Verifies the outcome: LCP element in field data, hero request start in the waterfall, field CLS for the route
